Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. As you all know, yesterday the High-Level Political Forum started at UN Headquarters in New York, and today it's an honor to welcome the President of ECOSOC, Ambassador Ray, who will brief you on the 2 weeks HLPF and also will also brief you on the progress around the Sustainable Development Goals. So, Ambassador, I give you the floor.

It's working fine. Thank you very much. It's good to be with you. This is a a period in the United Nations calendar that is really the largest gathering that we have to look specifically at the Sustainable Development Goals. It's a gathering not only of member states, both members of delegations but also in the second week ministerial presence from a number of countries. It also includes an extraordinary number of representatives of civil society who are with us all in all of our meetings as active participants. And so we will be seeing throughout this building, but other side meetings, there's over 190 side meetings taking place throughout the next 2 weeks. It's going to be a major effort on our part to assess how we're doing with respect to the critical issues of sustainability and achieving greater prosperity globally. It's also an opportunity for us to talk with some intensity about exactly how we're going to go as we, as we, as we must go forward. It's been 10 years since we've really started bringing people together to focus on the SDGs. We have also included opportunities for member states to tell us how they're doing, what we call VNR, national statements that are made about voluntary national reviews. 190 out of the 193 members have participated actively in that process, some as many as 3 times. And so it's been an opportunity for us to have an ongoing presentation about how we actually mobilize support and actually get to a place where we're making the progress that we need. do we need to make? Obviously, this is a time for taking stock. It's the halfway point. It's 5 years, 5 years to go until 2030. Having said that, I am always one of those people who reminds others that what comes— when people say to me, what comes after 2030, I say 2031. Life doesn't stop at 2030. We keep going. And how we keep going and in what form exactly we will keep going is something that we'll be discussing over the next several years as we lead up to the 2030 point. The key SDGs that we're looking at this year are on health and well-being, on gender equality. I just chaired a meeting on gender equality this morning. Decent work and economic growth, life below water, and the key role that partnerships play in achieving the goals. A couple of things I would just say. It's important to remember when a famous British politician was asked, you know, well, why didn't you achieve all the things you said you were going to achieve when you became Prime Minister? He said, events, my dear boy, events. And obviously we've been impacted by events. No, no plan that covers 10 years of history is going to be unaffected by what happens in the real world. And when it comes to looking at what's happened in our real world, let us recall the impact that COVID has had. Right. On every nation-state, on all national governments, as well as on the UN itself and on the global population. Let's realize and recognize that we're living in a period of conflict such as we have not seen around the world since 1945. This has obviously had a dramatic effect on global prosperity, on global GDP, on people's ability to make a living, on people's ability to survive. It's put costs up dramatically and it's had a tremendous effect. Climate change has continued to wreak havoc with our weather, with our ability to predict exactly how countries will be able to do. It's affected the mobility, the movement of people. We have more people now who are displaced in the world than we've ever had, displaced and homeless people. We have a record number in that unfortunate statistic. And so we need to understand that there's been lots of challenges, not created by member states, but just have been part of the framework in which we've all had to live and work. Having said that, I think it's important to stress, as the Secretary-General and President Lee did yesterday, of actually giving an assessment that says, well, here's where things have improved, and we've seen significant areas of improvement. We've reduced childhood mortality quite substantially in the last 5 years. We've had major success on improving maternal and childhood health. These have been very significant. We have more women going to school than ever before, more girls participating in the education system. We can point to— many areas in which we're in fact not necessarily on track, but where we have improved compared to where we were before. It's not a litany of failure. It's, if you like, it's a way of saying the glass is not completely full. We've not achieved everything we would have liked to have been able to achieve, but it's a story where we need to improve on the areas where we have fallen behind, and I think we all know where those are and what it's going to take to get there. 2 other points I would make on that score. One of them is this is a process driven by nation states. The agreement to establish the Sustainable Development Goals was not a decision made by the Secretariat of the UN. Or by the agencies of the UN. It was a decision taken by the member states of the UN. And so it's important for us to continue the, uh, the process of insisting that it's, it's only when nation-states take real ownership of the Sustainable Development Goals in all of their aspects that we are actually able to make substantial progress. It will be a knee-jerk reaction to say, oh, that's the UN's fault. The UN said this was going to happen and it didn't happen. No, that's not— that's not an accurate description of what happened. The nations of the world, united for some purposes and not always for others, that the nations of the world agreed that they in fact would accept these goals as their goals, that they would be goals that they would take seriously, that they would apply, that they would measure, and that they would then do their best to change and shift policies to make it happen. At the same time, it must be said that some decisions that have been taken with respect to the global economy And decisions that have been taken with respect to the funding of the critical institutions that we have created since 1945 have and are having a negative impact on the ability of countries to achieve what has to be achieved. So it isn't just a matter of saying, oh, it's all about something else out there called climate change, or it's all about something that's, you know, not financing for development that hasn't happen sufficiently, these things are happening because nation states that are polluting are not taking the steps to stop pollution. And these things are happening because nation states that have the means to provide greater support for sustainable development have chosen not to do so for their own domestic reasons. And that also represents a significant challenge for all of us and for the global system. A retreat from global solidarity will have a negative impact on our ability to improve the lives of the people of the world. And this is why we have to continue to urge all member states to participate as fully as possible in the achievement of these goals, but also in taking the steps that will allow the goals to be achieved by financing agencies properly, by financing development properly, and providing member states with the means to actually achieve the goals that we think are important. These are the themes that we'll be discussing for the next 2 weeks. It's going to be a great opportunity, I think, for people who watch UNTV and other other ways of looking and seeing how these issues are being discussed and how the debate unfolds. So I'll be glad to take any questions. Si vous avez des questions en anglais ou en français, happy to do that. Yes, please.

Thank you very much, Ambassador Wray, on behalf of the United Nations Correspondents Association for doing this briefing. My name is Edith Lederer from the Associated press. The Secretary General has repeatedly talked about backsliding on gender equality, and I wonder if you could tell us a little more about what this meeting this morning was saying about the fight to achieve gender equality, which I believe the Secretary-General said was going to take 300 years? And also, could you tell us how you envision the U.S. withdrawal from the World Health Organization impacting the health goal in the SDGs?

Thank you.

Thank you.

Well, I'm going to get into trouble by disagreeing with the Secretary-General. I don't think a statistic that says, you know, we're not going to get there for 300 years, I don't think that helps because I don't actually think it's accurate in the sense that you can extrapolate from any one year or one trend and say, well, if this doesn't change, then look at what's going to happen. Yeah, you can do that, but the reality is we are making remarkable progress on women's equality around the world. And that was one of the things that was discussed very actively in the group this morning. There are— there is a very active debate. There is a pushback, which the Secretary-General has accurately described, from a number of nation-states on the issue of gender equality and on the issue of how we measure it and on the the measures that we have to take to advance it. But my interpretation of current events and of global history is that the drive for global equality between women and men is unstoppable. And it will increase and it will increase and it will increase. And we're seeing social changes in a number of countries around the world where it is women's equality and and the growth in women's equality which is actually helping to transform those economies. And in the discussion that we heard this morning, member states from all over the world were describing the level of commitment of their governments and the extent to which they were prepared to measure exactly how they're doing and how they're building gender equality into the very fiber of their national legislation and their national legal structures. So yes, misogyny is still around and reactionary people are still around and some of them are in government in different parts of the world, but they're not going to succeed. I mean, I firmly believe that the drive for women's equality is unstoppable and that's as it should be and as it must be because gender equality is one of the goals that allows the other goals to be achieved. And that's where I think the profoundly catalytic impact of gender equality on achieving greater prosperity is undeniable. And we've seen this in development study after development study and looking at the advanced economies, looking at other places. The more we reinforce the principle that men and women are equal and they need to be treated equally and fairly in the workplace, in laws, in their rights to hold property, in their rights to make economic decisions, in their rights to participate fully in the economy, in their quest for dignity and their right to dignity. Those studies show very clearly that the countries that embrace that actually achieve greater economic growth and greater prosperity. So I think that's very clear. Um, as, as the president of the Economic and Social Council, I deeply regret any decision by a country, any country, to withdraw from any of the work of the United Nations. And I, I do think that a country is as important to the global system as the United States. To see them withdraw from the World Health Organization is deeply regrettable, and it is important for us to do everything we can to allow the WHO to do the work that it needs to do, facing up to the fact that a withdrawal of funding from the United States invariably will have an impact on the organization. I was actually in Geneva last week and had a meeting with, uh, with Dr. Tedros, and it was a very good meeting that I had with him. And he was, um, he was pointing out how the WHO had had to make a number of challenging decisions about restructuring itself, restructuring its organization, accepting the fact that there were going to be reductions and cuts, and then pointing out that the work of the WHO is going to continue and the mandate of the WHO is going to continue and the work that has to be done will be done. But let us, let us recognize that it's, it's not a great day when the United States decides to withdraw from the WHO, but it's not the end of the WHO and And frankly, it's not the end of the world because we have to build organizations that are resilient enough to deal with the impact of short-term and, in my view, misguided political decisions by governments that are neither in the interests of their countries nor are they in the interest of anybody else's country. But the United States is free to do what it wishes to do. But for the rest of us, we have to ensure the resilience and the success of the United Nations, and we also have to make other changes in every institution that's being impacted by the cuts that were— that are being put in place. But building a resilient UN is the key to what we need to do over the next very short while.
Let's take some— additional questions. At the back, Chris.
Hi, Ambassador Rae. Nice to see you. Thank you for doing this briefing.
Thank you, Chris.

Chris Reyes with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Uh, 2 questions. Uh, the first, uh, is under the new Prime Minister, Prime Minister Carney, does Canada have any plans to expand or strengthen its role at the UN as a strategy to deal with tensions with the United States, especially as the US is increasingly critical of multilateralism, including the UN's Sustainable Goals? And somewhat related to that, Ambassador, I was just listening to the confirmation hearing of Mike Wallace, who is nominated for the UN Ambassador— the US's UN Ambassador. He was quite critical of the UN. What would be your message to the incoming U.S. Ambassador to the UN?
I look forward to working with Ambassador Welch if he's indeed confirmed. I think it's—
It's just the hearing.

I know, just the hearing, but I mean, I'm just saying if he is confirmed, and it's not for me to say, but I— like me, he comes from the political realm in his past, and he— understands how institutions work. I think he'll— I look forward— I hope he keeps an open mind about understanding the necessity of the work of much of what the UN does. And I think we all look forward to seeing him. It's been a while to get him here, and I'm looking forward to a chance to engage with him very directly. Prime Minister Carney has a long history of engagement with the UN and all of its institutions. He knows them well. I discussed it with him in my meeting with him last month, and he's— I think the government is reflecting on how it can encourage the kind of reforms that are necessary in the global system to make it work more effectively. And also how Canada needs to deepen its, its connections with the global system in all of its aspects. And that as a country, that's really what we've all been about. And yes, the United States is our most important trading partner, but it's by no means our only trading partner. And global solidarity is not just about trade, it's about healthcare, it's about climate change, it's about dealing with conflict around the world, and it's about advancing the interests and values of all of our countries. And so I, I think the Prime Minister has a very outward-looking view about Canada's future and our future with the United Nations and with other multilateral institutions of which we have traditionally been very supportive.

Hi, Ambassador Xu Deji with China Central Television. I have a general question here. We know the current difficult situation in the United Nations. Has that financial difficulty impacted the high-level political forum this year? And given the fact that more and more people are starting doubting the, you know, the whole UN system, now. How do you— how would you expect governments to hear those ideas from this forum? Thank you.

Well, let's deal with the facts. First of all, the challenges facing the UN are the challenges that have been created by nation states. When 2 of the largest nation states either don't pay their dues or won't pay them on time for whatever reason, it affects the liquidity of the United Nations, of the Secretariat, of our United Nations' ability to do its job. So who do you blame for that? Do you blame the United Nations? I don't think so. I think you hold nation-states to account for the fact that they have not been supportive. The UN's financial problems are not the fault of the UN. The UN is not overspending money. I mean, look at the needs that people have that are not being met, even when the UN is fully funded, even when all the budgets are funded of the UN. Those budgets do not cover the real needs of, of the world, of what people— what people need to get out of poverty, what people need to be able to feed their families, and what we need to create a more prosperous world. So let's hold to account the people who should be held to account. It's the member states who have to take responsibility. And yes, some member states more than others. The 2 largest donors to the— to the— not donors, the 2 largest assessed contributions, taxes to be paid to the UN, who have not been paying their taxes, are China and the United States. And they're 2 members of the Security Council. So who We have to have a much more candid conversation about who is responsible for what. And the UN is going through dramatic changes. Its agencies are having to make decisions to lay people off, make cuts, do all kinds of difficult things. I've been spending the last 2 months in my role as Chairman of EXOC meeting with the heads of all the agencies here in New York, in Geneva, in Vienna, in Nairobi, wherever they find themselves trying to figure out— help people figure out how do we create a stable structure to deal with this— these cuts. These cuts are not the result of some abstract act of God. They're results of the acts of nation states who have political leaders who've made decisions to underfund and to not live up to their responsibilities. In Canada, you know, we have laws in Canada that require, uh, people who don't pay child support to pay it. And the name for the people who don't pay child support is deadbeat dads. And we have a lot of deadbeat dads in this, in this organization at the moment— member states who do not pay their dues. And do not live up to their responsibilities, and that's something we have to deal with.
Sorry, you didn't answer my question. How would that impact this year's—
Not at all. No, HLPF continues. It's fully funded, and we've got active participation from civil society. It's going to be a very full and fulsome and engaged meeting.
Next question.

Thank you, Mr.

Ambassador. My name is Volodymyr Uchenko, National News Agency of Ukraine, Ukrinform. Could you be more specific about how Russia's aggression against Ukraine is affecting the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals?

Well, looking back— thank you for your question— looking back to what happened with the invasion of Ukraine, That caused an immediate food crisis, international food crisis, caused an immediate increase in the price of food for billions of people. It caused the displacement of millions of people internally in Ukraine and then externally to other countries. So the population of Ukraine was reduced dramatically, and the question of how do you help and deal with, you know, this, this level of forcible displacement became a huge, a huge issue. So the, the, the knock— what we call the knock-on effects, the, the consequences of what Russia has done and is still doing on the global economy has been consistently negative. And we've had to make every step to to try and make sure that people have enough food, that the price of food is affordable. The inflation spike seems to have— has come down. I think one has to recognize that that has come down. But let's not forget, it did have a profoundly negative impact when it happened. And it's, it's proof of the— there's a famous poem written many years ago, 400 years ago, by a British, a British poet who wrote it. What was it? poem that said, no man is an island. No country is an island, unique unto itself. When things impact, it impacts or felt much more widely than we realize. And I wouldn't describe it as a ripple effect. It's more like a tsunami effect because of the impact that it had at the time. And there's no getting around that. But it's also true to say that the global economy is resilient and the Ukrainian economy is resilient and the Ukrainian people are resilient. And hopefully the resilience of Ukraine's friends will be sufficient to allow Ukraine to succeed in its self-defense.
I have one question from Pamela Falk, who is online. Pamela?

Yes, thank you very much, Paul. Thank you, Ambassador Rae, for all of these comments and the briefing. On a big picture question, as a follow-up to the CBC question, I asked this to the Secretary-General yesterday. Given the complaints around the world, not of any particular country, but of every country, or several, on the stalemates at the UN, on antisemitism, on spending issues, which is being addressed. How do you think the UN can get a better reputation? Is it communications? Is it messaging? Because it's trending downward globally in terms of the perception of what the UN can do? And then I have a little follow-up.

Well, I mean, Pamela, let me take you on a little bit. Again, I've now been here for 5 years, so I don't know how much longer I've got, so I might as well have a good time. That's sort of my thinking at the moment. No, seriously, I think there is a systematic ideological attack on the United Nations, and I think it would be a foolish person who would say that's not happening. And these ideological misinformation, disinformation, propaganda is carried by social media. It's amplified around the world, and it Is it having an effect? Of course it's having an effect. And that's why I think it's important for us to set— when you say, do we have to communicate better? Absolutely. We have to communicate all the time. We have to tell people what we're doing. The needs of the world are much greater than the United Nations can deal with because it simply doesn't have the financial means to respond to that. So you will have You will have people who will blame the United Nations because they say we're not getting enough, and then you'll have people saying to the United Nations, well, yeah, but you're spending money over here, you're not spending it over there. I think one has to recognize that in a $100 trillion-plus economy GDP every year, the United Nations is a very, very tiny proportion of that. minuscule proportion in terms of its budget. Where I think we need to do a better job is I think we have to do a better job in communicating. I think that's fair enough. Everybody does. It's a fair comment about everybody. Everybody needs to communicate better. The biggest— the worst assumption you can ever make, as George Bernard Shaw once said, about communication is assuming that it's already happened. We all assume that people know what we're doing. They don't necessarily— we have to tell them and explain it. But the second thing that's really critical is, yes, the UN has to restructure. The UN has to make changes because of the very, very widespread cuts in revenue which we are seeing. A drop in revenue to the Secretariat from the assessed contributions and a major drop in revenue from the voluntary contributions. That are going to the UN and all of its agencies. As Guy Ryder pointed out in his talk in the middle of June, those cuts are in the neighborhood— roughly speaking, going from a budget around $70 billion to a number that's now in the $40s. That's over a $25 billion cut, and that is affecting all aspects of the UN. But the effort to deal with this has got to be priority number one for all of the agencies and for the Secretary-General and his team and for all of us as member states. This getting the UN into a position where it can be resilient to these shocks, where it can also be only spending the money that it has, which it It's all it can do. Don't forget, the UN can't borrow. The UN financial system for the Secretariat makes no sense because if you give late to the— if you pay late to the UN, it's to your advantage as a member state because you get the money back at the end of the year because not only can the UN not borrow, it also can't pass money from one year to the next. So, I mean, if you, you know, if you said, was this, was this, uh, financial system brilliantly conceived, I would say only brilliantly conceived if you didn't want it to succeed, because it's, it's not designed— the current financial system of the UN is not designed for success. The UN is not a government. It can't tax. It relies on the assessments coming from member states. And if member states are not prepared to pay those assessments, which they are supposed to pay as a condition of membership, then what do you think is going to happen? Going to be less money, less effectiveness. But you can't just complain about that. You also have to say, okay, that's— this is the hand we've been dealt, and we'd better deal with it, and we'd better play it as well as we can. And that's, I think, something that all of us We have to be up to our game, and this is going to become clear over the next several months as to our ability to respond to this crisis effectively.

I'm really sorry, but the President has another commitment, so we have to close this press briefing. But I will be able to take your questions aside, and then we'll see how we can respond to them. But to all of you, thank you for coming today. It's the end of the press briefing. Thank you.
